blocks.prompt: The Cat That Lives in a Family
blocks.text: There are about forty kinds of wild cat in the world. Almost every one of them hunts alone. A tiger walks its forest by itself. A leopard drags its meal up a tree so it can eat in peace. The lion is the exception. Lions live in a group called a pride, and a pride is really a family of related females. Grandmothers, mothers, sisters, aunts, and cousins stay together their whole lives. The cubs grow up in a pile, drinking milk from any mother who will let them. The lionesses do most of the hunting, and they hunt as a team. One lioness circles wide to push the herd. The others wait in the grass where the herd will run. Even so, most hunts fail. Only about one in four ends in a meal. The males look impressive with their manes, but their job is different. They walk the edges of the family's land and roar into the dark. That roar carries five miles. It is not a warning for the pride. It is a message to every lion outside it.

blocks.prompt: The Exception in the Cat Family
blocks.text: The cat family is a family of loners. Roughly forty species of wild cat prowl the planet, and almost all of them hunt by themselves, meet only to mate, and go their separate ways. The lion is the exception, and biologists have argued for decades about why. A pride is not a random crowd. It is a family of related lionesses: sisters, mothers, daughters, cousins, who are born into the pride and usually stay for life. Their cubs are raised communally. Lionesses often give birth within weeks of each other and will nurse each other's cubs, so a cub can feed from an aunt without much fuss. The males are visitors. Young males are pushed out of their birth pride at around two or three and spend years as nomads, often traveling with their brothers in a group called a coalition. If a coalition is strong enough, it takes over a pride and holds it. Tenure is short. Two or three years later, a stronger coalition arrives and the cycle repeats. Hunting is cooperative, and it is harder than it looks. Lionesses spread out, some driving prey forward while others wait in the grass. Even with teamwork, roughly three out of four hunts end with nothing. A pride survives on the rare success and on whatever it can steal from hyenas. Then there is the mane. It looks like armor, but researchers who studied lions in the Serengeti found it works mainly as a signal. Lionesses paid more attention to darker manes, and rival males were more reluctant to approach them. A dark mane advertises a well fed, healthy animal, and it does so from a distance, before anyone has to fight.

blocks.prompt: Why One Cat Learned to Live Together
blocks.text: Every cat is a solitary hunter, or nearly every cat. Of roughly forty wild cat species, the lion alone builds a permanent society. That single exception has occupied biologists for half a century, because sociality is expensive. A pride shares every kill, so each lioness eats less than she would alone. Cooperative hunting does not clearly pay for itself either: a lioness hunting alone often does about as well per meal as one hunting in a group. So why gather at all? The strongest answer is real estate. In the Serengeti, prides do not defend hunting grounds so much as they defend the good ones: river confluences, thick cover near water, the places where prey must eventually come. Those sites are scarce and worth fighting for, and a lone lioness cannot hold one. A group can. The pride, in this reading, is less a hunting party than a standing army built around a piece of land. Defense also explains the cubs. When a new coalition of males takes over a pride, it usually kills the cubs fathered by the previous males. It is brutal and it is arithmetic: a nursing lioness will not conceive, and the incoming males may hold the pride for only two or three years before they are driven out. Killing the cubs returns the females to breeding within days. Lionesses resist. They hide their litters, they fight, and they raise their cubs together in a creche, which is far harder for a strange male to break up than a single mother alone. Even the mane is a compromise rather than a triumph. Researchers in Tanzania used life sized dummy lions to test it, and found that lionesses approached the dark maned dummy while rival males avoided it. A dark mane broadcasts condition. But dark fur absorbs heat, and dark maned males run measurably hotter in the sun. The lion carries an advertisement it cannot take off. The species is thinner on the ground than most people assume. A century ago perhaps two hundred thousand lions ranged across Africa and into Asia. Today, somewhere around twenty thousand remain, almost all in Africa, plus several hundred Asiatic lions confined to one forest in India. The most recognizable animal on Earth occupies a fraction of the ground it once held.

blocks.prompt: The Cat That Broke the Rule
blocks.text: The cat family is, almost to a species, solitary. A tiger holds a territory alone. A leopard hauls its kill into a tree to eat away from everything that would take it from him. Of the roughly forty wild cats, exactly one has built a permanent society, and the puzzle of why has run for fifty years without a clean ending. Start with what does not explain it. The obvious answer is hunting: many mouths bring down big prey. It sounds right, and the data refuse to cooperate. Long term work in the Serengeti found that a lioness hunting alone often takes home as much meat per meal as one hunting in a group, because whatever the team gains in success it gives back at the carcass, where everyone eats. The classic paper on the question is titled, bluntly, Why lions form groups: food is not enough. Group living costs a lioness food. Something else must be paying her back. The best current answer is land. Prides do not defend hunting range at large; they defend particular pieces of it. River confluences, the thick cover at a bend, the last reliable water in a dry season: these are the sites prey must come to, and they are rare. A lioness cannot hold one by herself. Three sisters can, and their daughters will inherit it. Seen this way a pride is not a hunting party. It is a lineage occupying real estate, and the hunting is incidental. Sociality also creates its own dangers, which sociality then has to solve. Male lions are not pride members in the way females are. They arrive as a coalition, often brothers, take a pride by force, and hold it for two or three years before a stronger coalition removes them. A new coalition typically kills the cubs it finds. This is not gratuitous. A nursing lioness does not conceive, and the males' tenure is shorter than the time those cubs need. Killing them returns the females to breeding almost immediately. The lionesses answer in kind: they synchronize their births, they pool their cubs into a creche and defend it collectively, and a pride of massed mothers is a far worse proposition for an incoming male than a single female with a litter. Much of what looks like lion family warmth is a countermeasure. Even the mane turns out to be a bargain rather than a gift. Researchers in Tanzania built life sized dummy lions with interchangeable manes and watched what real lions did. Lionesses approached the dark maned dummies. Rival males kept away from them. The mane is not armor; it is a billboard, and what it advertises is condition, readable across open grass before anyone commits to a fight. The cost is thermal. Dark fur absorbs more heat, and dark maned males measurably run hotter. In a hot country, the better a lion advertises, the more he suffers for it. Then the roar, which carries about five miles. That range is not simply a matter of lung power. In most mammals the vocal folds are triangular and need considerable pressure to vibrate. In lions and tigers, the folds are squared off and loaded with fat, and they flap under low pressure like a flag rather than snapping like a rubber band. These cats also trade a fully hardened hyoid bone for an elastic ligament, which gives the larynx room to work. A lion is loud less because it pushes harder than because its instrument is shaped for it. None of this has helped much. Perhaps two hundred thousand lions lived across Africa, the Middle East, and India a century ago. Roughly twenty thousand remain, plus several hundred Asiatic lions in a single Indian forest. A growing share of the survivors live in fenced reserves, managed, counted, and trucked between fences to keep the bloodlines from narrowing. The animal that organized itself around holding ground now holds it because we have drawn a line around it.
